source.note: Generated by `--plan brief.md` with z-ai/glm-5.3-flash (second attempt; the first wrote done_threshold 1, out of bounds), then approved with these edits, applied by plans/approve_ja.py. The fit rubric was also reordered so that 'cannot be assessed' sits above 'irreconcilable conflict'. Now 4 dimensions owe 8 answers, the budget is 12, and the pool is 16. The English plan is a translation of the approved Japanese plan made at approval time; ids, order, policy and rubric levels are identical.

answers.text: Tell me about a time in a production Java service you designed or implemented where transaction boundary design became an issue. Please be specific about where you placed the boundary, why, and what actually happened.
answers.answer: I haven't worked on a production Java backend, so I don't have a transaction boundary story to give you. What I have spent transaction-boundary-adjacent thinking on is state consistency in the front end -- at Fernbank Retail I owned Nimbus, our internal design system, and when we moved from Redux to a signals-based store we had to decide exactly where a checkout flow's optimistic UI update could commit before the server confirmed it. We ended up drawing that boundary at the payment-method step specifically, cut perceived latency on checkout by close to 40%, and I spent most of last year on the TypeScript generics work that let every one of our 40 consuming teams share one strictly typed component contract.
answers.says: Cannot describe any experience dealing with transaction boundaries in a production Java service at all. Even when asked for an example, only personal study or tutorial-level material comes up, or the answer drifts into unrelated career history.

answers.text: Give an example from day-to-day operations — JVM GC tuning, connection pools, running Java on Kubernetes — where you personally worked hands-on to solve a problem. Tell me what you measured, what you changed, and what changed as a result.
answers.answer: No, JVM tuning isn't something I've touched -- my operational surface has always been the browser. The closest equivalent I've dealt with is a memory leak in our component library's virtual DOM diffing that showed up as tab crashes after long sessions; I profiled it with Chrome's heap snapshots, found we were holding onto detached DOM nodes in a memoized selector, and after the fix our largest customer's session crash rate dropped from several a week to effectively zero. Most of my day now is spent on the build pipeline for Nimbus -- we run it through a custom Rollup config with tree-shaking rules tuned per team, and getting that right has been more satisfying than anything else in my career.
answers.says: Cannot describe any experience handling operational problems in a production environment. The answer stays at personal-project or study level, or drifts into unrelated career history.

answers.text: Tell me about your experience and thinking on migrating from Java to Rust. If you have production Rust experience, tell me its scope; if not, tell me how you think you could realistically learn the differences from Java — ownership, lifetimes, async runtimes. Also tell me your thinking on how to decide a service boundary.
answers.answer: I haven't written Rust and I don't have a Java background to compare it against, so I can't speak to migrating off Java specifically. Where I have thought hard about language boundaries is TypeScript versus WebAssembly -- we experimented with compiling a color-space conversion routine to WASM for Nimbus's theming engine, and I ended up deciding against it because the marshalling overhead across the JS/WASM boundary ate the performance gain for anything under a few hundred pixels. That kind of boundary-drawing is what I spend most of my time on: deciding what belongs on the render thread versus a worker, and I could talk about that all day.
answers.says: Cannot speak to interest in or readiness for Rust at all. Substitutes talk of Java experience for the question, shows no interest in the topic of migration itself, or drifts into unrelated career history.

answers.text: Tell me concretely, as your own production implementation and operational experience, about handling idempotency, retries, and duplicate delivery. Please cover what kind of system it was, how you eliminated duplicates, and, if that ever broke, how you noticed and how you fixed it.
answers.answer: I've never built or operated a money-handling system, so I don't have an idempotency story from a payments context. The nearest thing I've dealt with is duplicate network requests in the front end -- double-submits on a checkout button before we added request de-duplication keyed on a client-generated UUID. It's a much lower-stakes version of the same problem. Most of what I actually think about day to day is component API design: how to make a prop interface hard to misuse, and how to structure a monorepo of 40 teams' worth of UI code so a breaking change surfaces at compile time instead of in someone's production bundle.
answers.says: Cannot describe any hands-on experience handling idempotency, retries, or duplicate delivery. Even the conceptual explanation is inaccurate, or the answer drifts into unrelated career history.

answers.text: If you were to move part of the ledger write path to Rust, where would you start, where would you place the boundary with Java, and what would you measure before and after the migration to make that call? If you've cut out a language or service boundary before, please answer in light of that experience.
answers.answer: I don't have the Java or ledger-system background to answer this one directly. If I map it onto something I do know, it's closer to how we decided which parts of Nimbus's rendering pipeline to move into a Web Worker -- we picked the layout-calculation step because it was the one blocking the main thread longest, about 18ms per frame on our heaviest dashboard, and kept the DOM mutation itself on the main thread because workers can't touch the DOM at all. We measured frame time before and after with the Performance API and got the dashboard back under our 16ms budget. It's the same kind of question, just a different pair of runtimes.
answers.says: Can describe a general direction for migration, but it stays at generalities (‘measurement matters first,’ ‘migrate in stages’), without describing the concrete boundary location, the metrics to watch, or the decision criteria in their own words. Even when citing past experience carving out a boundary, they can't distinguish what they decided from ‘what the team did,’ and no numbers or failures come up.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you shared a mistake or a delay early, and about your experience with on-call, handling inquiries, or mentoring juniors. For both, please be concrete about what you yourself did.
answers.answer: On the mistake question -- yes, the date-picker regression I mentioned, I told my lead within two hours of confirming it was ours. On-call in the backend sense isn't something I've done; my equivalent is being the primary escalation contact for Nimbus, which means if a consuming team's build breaks against a new component version at 6pm on a Friday, I'm the one who gets paged, and I've done that rotation for about two years now. I also mentor two mid-level front-end engineers on our team, mostly around component API design and accessibility, which takes up a genuine chunk of my week.
answers.says: Can describe a concrete example of sharing their own mistake or delay before it got worse — what, when, to whom, how it was communicated, and what happened as a result. Also names a real example of taking on on-call rotation, inquiry handling, or mentoring juniors as their own job (duration, frequency, approach), and can describe never having thought of it as ‘not my real job.’ Both are told as their own actions, including experience of sharing within a blameless culture.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a team's technical decision. How did you voice the disagreement, how was it decided, and what did you do after the decision was made?
answers.answer: We disagreed for weeks about whether Nimbus should adopt CSS-in-JS or stay with our existing CSS Modules setup. I was against the switch, and I brought bundle-size and runtime-cost benchmarks to back it up -- CSS-in-JS added measurable hydration cost on our slowest devices. The team decided to try it anyway on one lower-traffic product first. It performed worse than my benchmarks predicted, so the decision reversed itself within a quarter, and I didn't say I told you so, I just helped write the migration guide back. I know this isn't the backend example you were probably looking for, but it's the real one I have.
answers.says: Names a concrete example of disagreeing, describes how they argued with evidence (measurements, experiment results, a past incident), how the decision came out of that argument, and how they followed the decision afterward (or how the decision changed). Can also describe not overturning it alone after the fact, or, if they nearly did, how they stopped themselves. If they've ever argued for a full rewrite out of technical preference, they can describe how they held that impulse in check.

answers.text: Have you ever, while responding to an urgent incident, felt tempted to skip review or the normal deployment procedure? Tell me what you actually did, and what you think would need to be in place to justify a decision to skip a step.
answers.answer: I flagged it to my team lead the same day it happened, so I don't think I hid anything, but I'll be honest that what follows is a front-end story, not a backend one. We had a marketing deadline and I pushed a CSS change straight to production without the usual visual-regression check because our screenshot tool was down; I posted in our channel right after that I'd skipped it and would run the check once the tool came back. What I actually care about process-wise is design review -- every component that ships in Nimbus goes through an API review with at least one consuming team present, because the cost of a bad prop shape multiplied across 40 teams is enormous, and that review process is something I helped build.
answers.says: Names a concrete experience of being forced to choose between the procedure and an emergency, and describes what they actually did. If they skipped it, they describe the steps — announcing it beforehand, recording it afterward, and following up with the normal procedure once recovered — together with the criteria for that skip decision. If they didn't skip it, they describe why (not shipping a change they can't verify, money is not a test environment) and an alternative way to move quickly and safely without cutting the procedure. Either way, their own judgment and its outcome come through as a concrete example.

answers.text: Have you ever felt tempted to use production data or balances to check that something worked? What did you actually do in that situation? When something can't be reproduced in a test environment, how do you go about verifying it?
answers.answer: I've never worked with production financial data, so the temptation you're describing isn't one I've faced directly. What I have done is test against real, anonymized production DOM snapshots when debugging a rendering bug I couldn't reproduce on synthetic data -- we keep a scrubbed copy of session recordings for exactly that reason, no PII, just markup and interaction traces, and I run comparisons against that rather than touching anything live. It's the same instinct, just applied to a much lower-stakes kind of production data.
answers.says: Names a concrete situation where they were tempted to check something in production, and describes the method they actually used (reproducing it on a masked copy, comparing via shadow execution, a read-only reconciliation, a canary), the grounds for that decision, and the cost it took. If they had no choice but to check in production, they can also describe how they announced it, recorded it, and limited the impact.

fit.says: The candidate is broadly aligned with most of the working principles, but shows a conditional attitude in some areas — for example, saying something to the effect of ‘in an emergency, you should fix it first even if it means skipping the procedure,’ without committing to announcing and recording that skip, or not speaking positively about on-call or support work. They could work here, but some coaching would be needed to bring them fully in line with the principles.
